title.text: Repeat a known number of times

introduces.label: loop that checks at the end

runs.text: Choosing the loop is answering two questions: do I know how many passes there will be? Does the first pass always happen?
The problem
The maths club wants a program that says whether a number is
prime
: a number greater than 1 that can only be divided exactly by 1 and by itself.
How does the program find out?
Try it
Decide by hand whether 7, 9, 2 and 1 are prime.
7 yes. 9 no: 9 = 3 × 3. 2 yes: it is the only even prime. 1 no: by definition, a prime has to be greater than 1.
Understand

relation.text: it is prime if it is greater than 1 and no number from 2 to the one before it divides it exactly.

examples.text: 2 → prime (there are no divisors to try).
1 → not prime (it is not greater than 1).

runs.text: 2 and 1 are the edge cases: with 2 there is no divisor to try, and 1 is left out by the definition.
Plan

entries.text: Try each possible divisor, from 2 to the number before.
If any divides exactly, the number is not prime.

runs.text: You have to remember whether any divided exactly, and that box has a new role:

description.text: Starts at a boolean value and changes only once, when something happens: that is how it remembers it happened.

flag

This time you know beforehand how many passes there will be: one for each possible divisor. That changes which loop suits.
The new tool
A
counted loop
is used when you know how many passes there will be.
carries its own counter, which starts at one value and moves up to another:

figure.description: A line with the values 1 to 6. The control starts at 1 and moves one by one; 5, the final value, is still included; on reaching 6 the loop ends.

caption.text: The control walks the values from the initial one to the final one, both included. When it goes past the final value, the loop ends.

runs.text: 1, 5 and the step 1 are computed. The control starts at 1.
Every round writes a line and adds the step: 2, 3, 4…
With the control at 5 the body still runs: the final value is included.
The control reaches 6, which is past the final value. The loop ends.

blocks.title: The 7 times table
blocks.source:
Algorithm SevenTable
  For i <- 1 To 3 Do
    Write 7 * i;
  EndFor
EndAlgorithm

runs.text: A
loop that checks at the end
always makes at least one pass:
runs its body and only then asks
. It is useful, for example, to ask for a value until it is valid:

figure.description: On the left, While: first the question and then the body, which can run zero times. On the right, Repeat: first the body and then the question; with False it repeats and with True it leaves, so the body runs at least once.

caption.text: the body comes before the question. Even if the condition already holds, the body runs once.

runs.text: With counted loops another very common role appears: the
best so far
, which keeps the highest (or lowest) value seen up to that moment.

description.text: Keeps the highest value seen; when a greater one arrives, it replaces it. It starts with the first value.

blocks.title: Is it prime?

runs.text: The flag starts at
: that way 1, 0 and the negatives already start as not prime. With 2, the loop goes from 2 to 1 and makes zero passes: the flag stays true, which is right.
Test
With 97, which is prime, the loop tries the 95 divisors from 2 to 96. Keep that number: in the strategies lesson you will improve it.
Improve
In one sentence:
The program tries the divisors one by one and stops at the first one that divides exactly
Without
, 9 would make the 7 passes even though from the second one the answer is known. With
it makes 2. With large numbers, the difference shows.
What you learned

points.text: A counted loop is used when you know how many passes there will be.
A loop that checks at the end always makes at least one pass.
A flag is a boolean value that changes only once to remember that something happened.
The best so far keeps the highest (or lowest) value seen; it starts with the first value.
An early exit cuts the loop when the answer is already known.

Using a counted loop when you do not know how many passes there will be.
